evidence.text:
- Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the United States has implemented a broad sweep of sanctions focused on isolating Russia from the global financial system, reducing the profitability of its energy sector, and blunting its military edge.
- The United States began its 2022 barrage of sanctions by freezing $5 billion of the Russian central bank’s U.S. assets, an unprecedented move to prevent Moscow from using its foreign reserves to prop up the Russian ruble.
- In March 2022, Washington banned the import of Russian crude oil, liquified natural gas, and coal, and restricted U.S. investments in most Russian energy companies.
- In December of that year, the United States and its Group of Seven (G7) allies implemented rules aimed at capping the price that other importing countries, such as China and India, would pay for Russian crude oil.
- In 2024, the United States barred imports of Russian enriched uranium, cutting off a major source of revenue for Russia.
- The United States implemented these sanctions in tandem with the European Union (EU) and other partners.
- While the EU placed its own sanctions on Russian banks and individuals, including Putin, the bloc’s sanctions on Russian energy have proven the most contentious.
- In 2022, the EU announced an embargo on imports of most Russian crude oil and joined the G7 price cap; in early 2023, it imposed an additional ban on Russian refined oil products such as diesel and gasoline.

evidence.text:
- This article examines public support for international sanctions imposed by the European Union (EU) against Russia in response to the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
- In 2022, the EU implemented nine packages of restrictive measures under its sanctions regime against Russia.
- As the war continued, the EU expanded its sanctions, adopting a total of fourteen sanctions packages by mid-2024.
- The EU has been a notable actor in this area, regularly employing sanctions to address threatening actions by other states (Giumelli, 2017, p. 1063).
- When faced with a major war on its eastern border, triggered by Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the EU exceeded its previously self-imposed limits of action (which had been confined to economic sanctions and humanitarian aid).
- In a significant policy shift, the EU complemented economic sanctions against Russia by providing military equipment to Ukraine for the first time (Steiner et al., 2023; De la Baume & Barigazzi, 2022).
- The evolution of the EU sanctions regime against Russia between 2014 and 2024 highlights a gradual and then accelerated expansion of restrictive measures, both in scope and intensity.
- Initially, after the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014, the EU adopted moderate targeted sanctions—mainly individual measures (asset freezes and travel bans for implicated Russian officials and oligarchs) combined with initially limited sectoral restrictions (e.g. embargoes on arms and exports of sensitive technology)—designed to penalise violations of Ukrainian sovereignty and induce compliance with the Minsk agreements (Lepeu, 2025).

evidence.text:
- 127,350 measles cases were reported in the European Region for 2024 – double the number reported for 2023 and the highest number seen in the Region since 1997.
- Children under five accounted for more than 40 per cent of reported cases in the Region – comprising 53 countries in Europe and Central Asia.
- More than half of the reported cases required hospitalization.
- A total of 38 deaths have been reported, based on preliminary data received as of 6 March 2025.
- Following a backsliding in immunization coverage during the COVID-19 pandemic, cases rose significantly again in 2023 and 2024.
- The European Region accounted for one third of all measles cases globally in 2024.
- In 2023 alone, 500,000 children across the Region missed the first dose of the measles vaccine (MCV1) that should be given through routine immunization services.
- Romania reported the highest number of cases in the Region for 2024, with 30,692 cases, followed by Kazakhstan with 28,147 cases.
